Heard the learned counsel Sri. M.B. Chandrachooda for the revision petitioner and the learned
High Court Government Pleader.

2. Accused who suffered an Order of conviction in CC No.76/2011 for the offences punishable under Sections 279, 304-A of IPC read with Section 134(A) and (B) and 187 of the Indian Motor Vehicles Act and ordered to undergo imprisonment for a period of one year for the offence under Section 304-A of the Indian Penal Code, confirmed in Crl.A.No.41/2013 is the revision petitioner.

3. Facts in brief which are utmost necessary for disposal of the revision petition as under:
A complaint came to be lodged with Koratagere Police Station stating that on 1 7 . 1 2 . 2 0 1 0 a t a b o u t 1 0 . 0 0 N C : 2 0 2 4 : K H C : 5 1 0 7 1 p . m . , n e a r G .
Nagenahalli-Gollarahatti Gate, on Ooordigere-Koratagere Road, accused being the driver of a Tata Ace vehicle bearing No.KA-06-C-2174 came from Oordigere side towards Koratagere in a rash and negligent manner and dashed against a girl by name Varshini who had been to School trip and was returning to her village and waiting for a vehicle, whereby she suffered severe injuries almost on all parts of the body.
She was shifted to Koratagere Government Hospital at first instance.

Subsequently to Tumkur Government Hospital, wherein she died on next day at 12.30 a.m.,
4. Based on such complaint, police investigated the matter thoroughly and filed charge sheet against the accused for the aforesaid offences.
Plea of the accused was recorded after securing his presence.
Accused pleaded not guilt.
Therefore, trial was held.

5. In order to bring home the guilt of the accused, in all ten witnesses were examined by the prosecution as NC: 2024:KHC:51071 PWs.1 to 10 and placed on record as many as nine documents which are exhibited and marked as Exs.P1 to P9 comprising of Complaint, Spot Mahazar, Inquest Mahazar, PM report, IMV Report, FIR and the Spot Sketch.

6. Detailed cross-examination of prosecution witnesses did not yield any positive material so as to Sri Ramanjeya vs The State Of Karnataka on 10 December, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/183344925/
2 disbelieve the case of the prosecution.

sentences.text: In the cross- examination, the father of the deceased (Varshini) has specifically answered that the deceased along with her friends was waiting for another vehicle to return to their native on the left side of the road and at that juncture, the driver of the Tata Ace vehicle (accused) drove the same in a rash and negligent manner and dashed against the deceased.
7. On conclusion of recording of evidence of the prosecution, the learned Trial Judge recorded the accused statement as is contemplated under Section 313 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

Accused has denied all the NC: 2024:KHC:51071 incriminatory materials, but failed to offer any explanation whatsoever in the form of written submission as is contemplated under Section 313(4) of Cr.P.C. or by examining himself.

8. Thereafter, the learned Trial Magistrate heard the parties in detail and convicted the accused as aforesaid and sentenced as referred supra.
9.
Being aggrieved by the same, accused filed an appeal before the First Appellate Court in Crl.A.No.41/2013.

10. Learned Judge in the First Appellate Court after securing the records heard the parties in detail and on re- appreciation of the material on record, dismissed the appeal filed by the accused by its judgment dated 23.01.2015.
11. Being further aggrieved by the same, the accused is before this Court.

Learned counsel Sri. M.B. Chandrachooda for the revision petitioner reiterating the grounds urged in the petition contending that the material evidence on record is hardly sufficient to object the negligence on the part of the revision petitioner which has been lost sight of by both the Courts while convicting the accused for the aforesaid offences and sought for admitting the revision petition for further consideration.

13. Alternatively, the learned counsel Sri. M.B. Chandrachooda contended that in the event this Court upholding the Order of Conviction, sentence ordered by the learned Magistrate confirmed by the First Appellate Court for a period of one year for the offence under Section 304-A of IPC may be set-aside by enhancing the fine amount and reasonable amount can be granted as compensation to the father of the deceased.
Per contra, the Sri. Vinay Mahadevaiah, learned High Court Government Pleader supports the impugned order.

sentences.text: He further contended that the spot sketch marked at Ex.P9 would conclusively establish that the deceased Varshini was standing on the left side of the road after getting down from the bus after she returned from school trip.
Admittedly, road is wide enough so as to infer that there was an upcoming vehicle whereby accused has to bring the vehicle to the extreme left side of the road and accident is beyond human control.

Therefore, negligence on the part of the accused is well depicted from the oral and documentary evidence based on record resulting in the death of Varshini and therefore all the ingredients to attract the offences alleged against the accused stands established by placing cogent and convincing evidence on record which has been rightly re- appreciated by the learned Judge in the First Appellate Court while upholding the conviction order passed by the NC:
2024:KHC:51071 Trial Magistrate and sought for dismissal of the revision petition.

16. He further argued that the alternate submission cannot be countenance in law having regard to the principles of law enunciated in the State of Punjab v. Saurabh Bakshi reported in (2015)5 SCC 182 and sought for dismissal of the revision petition in toto.

sentences.text: 17. Having heard the arguments in detail, this Court perused the material on record meticulously.

18. On such perusal of the material on record, it is crystal clear that the PW1 is the eye witness to the incident so also the other prosecution witnesses who has supported the case of the prosecution.
Spot Mahazar coupled with the Spot Sketch would depict the place of incident and there is no dispute about the same.
19. Accused being the driver of the Tata Ace vehicle bearing No.KA-06-C-2174 is not in dispute.
Admittedly, NC: 2024:KHC:51071 Varshini (deceased) was standing on the left side of the road after getting down from the bus which had been to school trip.
Varshini and others were waiting for another vehicle to get back to their village.
At that juncture, the incident has occurred and PW1 has withstood the scorching cross-examination on behalf of accused.
20. Material evidence on record would also depict that there was no mechanical defects in the offending vehicle.

Crowning all these aspects of the matter, absolutely there is no explanation forth coming from the accused about the incident either in the form of written submissions or by explaining it orally or at least by examining himself as a witness.
21.
In a matter of this nature, there is a onerous responsibility on the accused to place his version of the incident on record.
It is no doubt true that the prosecution has to establish the charges leveled against the accused beyond reasonable doubt as in any other criminal case but - 10 - NC: 2024:KHC:51071

after prosecution places necessary evidence on record, the learned Trial Magistrate should put those incriminatory materials to the accused while recording the accused statement which is mandatory in nature.
In the case on hand, learned Trial Magistrate has recorded the accused statement by putting across the incriminatory material in a proper manner.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
Relevant paragraph of the said judgment is culled out hereunder for the sake of ready reference which reads as under:
"39.
It is true that the prosecution is required to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt but the provisions of Section 313 CrPC are not a mere formality or purposeless.

They have a dual purpose to discharge, firstly, that the entire material parts of the incriminating evidence should be put to the accused in accordance with - 11 - NC: 2024:KHC:51071 law and, secondly, to provide an opportunity to the accused to explain his conduct or his version of the case.
To provide this opportunity to the accused is the mandatory duty of the court.

If the accused deliberately fails to avail this opportunity, then the consequences in law have to follow, particularly when it would be expected of the accused in the normal course of conduct to disclose certain facts which may be within his personal knowledge and have a bearing on the case."
23.

Applying the above principles of law to the absence of any contra materials placed on record or the explanation offered by the accused, the learned Trial Magistrate appreciating the prosecution evidence and recording the Order of conviction for the aforesaid offences which has been rightly re-appreciated by the First Appellate Court, needs no interference that too in the revisional jurisdiction.

24. View of this Court is supported by the principles of law enansuated in the case of Amit Kapoor vs. Ramesh Chander and another reported in (2012) 9 SC 460.
- 12 - NC: 2024:KHC:51071 25.

sentences.text: Therefore, from the above discussion, conviction recorded by the Trial Magistrate, confirmed by the First Appellate Court needs no interference.
26. Having said thus, it is seen that the Trial Magistrate has imposed one year simple imprisonment for the offence punishable under Section 304-A of IPC.
No doubt, it is a discretionary order.

27. Relevant paragraphs of the Hon'ble Apex Court which is binding in nature while imposing the appropriate - 13 - NC: 2024:KHC:51071 sentence for the offence under Section 304-A of IPC is culled out hereunder;
14.

In this context, we may refer with profit to the decision in Balwinder Singh wherein the High Court had allowed the revision and reduced the quantum of sentence awarded by the Judicial Magistrate, First Class, for the offences punishable under Sections 304-A, 337, 279 IPC by reducing the sentence of imprisonment already undergone, that is, 15 days.

The Court referred to the decision in Dalbir Singh v. State of Haryanas and reproduced two paragraphs which we feel extremely necessary for reproduction:
(Balwinder Singh case, SCC pp. 186-87, para 12) "12.... 1.

entities.text: Dalbir Singh v. State of Haryanas
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: When automobiles have become death traps any leniency shown to drivers who are found guilty of rash driving would be at the risk of further escalation of road accidents.

All those who are manning the steering of automobiles, particularly professional drivers, must be kept under constant reminders of their duty to adopt utmost care and also of the consequences befalling them in cases of dereliction.
One of the most 9 effective ways of keeping such drivers under mental vigil is to maintain a deterrent element in the sentencing sphere.
Any latitude shown to them in that sphere would tempt them to make driving frivolous and a frolic.

Bearing in mind the galloping trend in road accidents in India and the devastating consequences visiting the victims and their families, criminal courts cannot treat the nature of the offence under Section 304-A IPC as attracting the benevolent provisions of Section 4 of the Probation of Offenders Act.
While considering the quantum of sentence to be imposed for the offence of causing death by rash or negligent driving of automobiles, one of the prime considerations should be deterrence.
A professional driver pedals the accelerator of the automobile almost throughout his working hours.
He must constantly inform himself that he cannot afford to have a single moment of laxity or inattentiveness when his leg is on the pedal of a vehicle in locomotion.

He cannot and should not take a chance thinking that a rash driving need not necessarily cause any accident; or even if any accident occurs it need not necessarily result in the death of any human being; or even if such death ensues he might not be convicted of the offence; and lastly, that even if he is convicted he would be dealt with leniently by the court.

He must always keep in his mind the fear psyche that if he is convicted of the offence for causing death of a human being due to his callous driving of the vehicle he cannot escape from a jail sentence.

This is the role which the courts can play, particularly at the Sri Ramanjeya vs The State Of Karnataka on 10 December, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/183344925/
6 level of trial courts, for lessening the high rate of motor accidents due to callous driving of automobiles.'

. In B. Nagabhushanam v. State of Karnataka the appellant was directed to undergo simple imprisonment for six months for the offence punishable under Section 304-A IPC.

State of Punjab10 was quoted: (B. Nagabhushanam case, SCC p. 735, para 16) "16....

sentences.text: Nevertheless, sentencing must have a policy of correction.
This driver, if he has to become a good driver, must have a better training in traffic laws and moral responsibility, with special reference to the potential injury to human life and limb.
Punishment in this area must, therefore, be accompanied by these components.
The State, we hope, will attach a course for better driving together with a livelier sense of responsibility, when the punishment is for driving offences.

Maybe, the State may consider, in case of men with poor families, occasional parole and reformatory courses on appropriate application, without the rigour of the old rules which are subject to Government discretion.
(Rattan Singh case 10, SCC pp. 720-21, para 5)"

28. On careful perusal of the aforesaid principles of law, it is crystal clear that the beneficial piece of legislation - 16 - NC: 2024:KHC:51071 namely Probation of Offenders' Act cannot be made applied where the accused is convicted for the offence under Section 304-A of IPC.
29.

Suffice to say that the material on record would warrant this Court to exercise its discretionary power in reducing the period of imprisonment from one year to six months by following the dictum of the Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of Saurabh Bhakshi supra by enhancing the fine amount in a sum of Rs.10,000/-.
30.
